title: Advanced String Algorithms
relevance: Pattern matching, duplicate substrings, and palindromes are staple SDE OA/interview topics where naive O(n·m) or O(n²) approaches fail and linear string algorithms are expected.

phases.goal: Establish why naive search is too slow and what LPS, Z-array, rolling hash, and Manacher each compute.

must_hit.point: Naive substring search takes O(n · m) time; KMP, Z-algorithm, and related methods achieve O(n + m) by avoiding re-examining characters via precomputed info or a rolling hash.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States naive is O(n·m) in n=text and m=pattern length, and names preprocessing (prefix/failure array) or rolling hash as the path to linear time.

must_hit.point: The KMP lps[i] value is the length of the longest proper prefix of pattern[0...i] that exactly matches a suffix of pattern[0...i]; a proper prefix is not the entire string, and lps[0] is always 0.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines LPS/failure function in terms of longest proper prefix that is also a suffix, and notes lps[0]=0.

must_hit.point: Z[i] stores the length of the longest substring starting at s[i] that is also a prefix of s.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives the Z-array definition as longest prefix-match length starting at each index i.

must_hit.point: Rabin–Karp compares a polynomial rolling hash of the pattern to each window of length m in the text, then verifies matches to resolve spurious collisions.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions hashing windows of length m, then character-by-character check when hashes collide.

probes: What does the KMP LPS array store, and how does that differ from what the Z-array stores at each index?

hints.1: One array is about prefixes that are also suffixes inside the pattern; the other compares each suffix-start to the whole string’s prefix.
hints.2: Name lps[i] for pattern[0...i] and Z[i] for the longest prefix of s that starts at i.
hints.3: lps[i] = longest proper prefix of pattern[0...i] that matches a suffix of that same substring; Z[i] = length of the longest substring starting at s[i] that matches a prefix of s.

phases.goal: Explain how LPS fallback, Z-window reuse, rolling-hash updates, and Manacher’s mirror radius actually advance without restarting from scratch.

must_hit.point: On LPS mismatch with len ≠ 0, fall back with len = lps[len - 1] instead of resetting to 0; for pattern "ABABACA" the final lps is [0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 0, 1].
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks the fallback (e.g. at 'C' in ABABACA: len goes lps[2]=1 then lps[0]=0) and cites the finished array [0,0,1,2,3,0,1].

must_hit.point: In KMP search, on mismatch the lps array repositions the pattern pointer j without backtracking the text pointer i; matching takes O(n) because i never decrements, and LPS build is O(m), for total O(n + m) time and O(m) space.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says i only moves forward; j = lps[j-1] on mismatch when j≠0; quotes O(n+m) time and O(m) LPS space.

must_hit.point: Z-algorithm keeps a rightmost match window [l, r]: if i > r compute naively; if i ≤ r set Z[i] = min(Z[i - l], r - i + 1) then try to extend past r and update [l, r].
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes the [l,r] window, the min(Z[i-l], r-i+1) init when inside the window, and extending/updating when matching beyond r.

must_hit.point: A rolling hash slides a window in O(1) by removing the leftmost contribution, multiplying by base B, adding the new rightmost character, and applying modulo; example with text "ABAC", m=2, B=10, M=97 yields window hashes 12, then 21, then 13.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists remove/shift/add/mod steps and can reproduce H=12 for "AB", 21 for "BA", 13 for "AC".

must_hit.point: Manacher maintains centre C and right boundary R of the rightmost palindrome; for i < R, P[i] is at least min(R - i, P[i_mirror]) where i_mirror = C - (i - C), then expand and update C,R if the palindrome extends past R.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names C, R, mirror formula, and min(R-i, P[i_mirror]) initialization before expanding.

probes: Walk through computing LPS for "ABABACA", then explain what KMP does with j on a mismatch during search.

hints.1: Start with i=1, len=0, lps[0]=0, and say what happens when pattern[i] ≠ pattern[len].
hints.2: On mismatch, set len = lps[len-1] (or j = lps[j-1] in search) rather than restarting the pattern from index 0 while leaving the text index alone.
hints.3: Final lps is [0,0,1,2,3,0,1]; in search, i never goes backward—only j is reset via LPS.

phases.goal: Choose among KMP/Z, Rabin–Karp, and Manacher versus simpler fallbacks based on the matching problem shape.

must_hit.point: For single pattern search, prefer KMP or Z-algorithm—both O(n+m) via preprocessing the pattern; Rabin–Karp is rarely faster for that case.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Picks KMP or Z for one pattern and notes Rabin–Karp is not usually faster for single-pattern matching.

must_hit.point: Prefer Rabin–Karp rolling hash for many queries, finding duplicate substrings, or multidimensional pattern matching because hashes compare lengths across starting positions flexibly.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names multi-pattern / duplicates / multidimensional as the rolling-hash sweet spot.

must_hit.point: For longest palindromic substring, Manacher is optimal O(n), but expand-around-centre O(n²) is the usual interview-acceptable fallback if Manacher details are forgotten.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts Manacher O(n) with expand-around-centre O(n²) as the practical interview substitute.

probes: When would you pick rolling hash over KMP or Z, and when is expand-around-centre enough instead of Manacher?

hints.1: Think about one pattern versus many windows/lengths/queries, and about palindrome-specific search.
hints.2: Single pattern → KMP/Z; duplicates/multi-query/multidimensional → Rabin–Karp; palindrome → Manacher or O(n²) expand.
hints.3: State: KMP/Z for single O(n+m) search; Rabin–Karp when hashing many substrings; Manacher O(n) for longest palindromic substring with expand-around-centre O(n²) as fallback.

phases.goal: Map LPS, Z-concatenation, rolling-hash binary search, and Manacher to concrete problem patterns.

must_hit.point: Longest happy prefix of s is exactly s.substr(0, lps[n-1])—the LPS value at the last index for the whole string.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says compute LPS of s and take the prefix of length lps[n-1].

must_hit.point: Shortest palindrome by adding in front: build combined = s + "#" + reverse(s); lps.back() is the longest palindromic prefix length of s; reverse the remaining suffix and prepend it. The "#" stops the prefix from overlapping the suffix beyond the original string’s length.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives the s+"#"+rev(s) construction, uses final LPS as palindromic-prefix length, and mentions the separator’s role.

must_hit.point: Z pattern search: combined = pattern + "$" + text; any i with Z[i] equal to pattern length is an occurrence (index adjusted relative to text).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes pattern+$+text and checking Z[i]==m for matches.

must_hit.point: Longest duplicate substring: binary search length L between 1 and n-1; for each L, rolling-hash all windows and verify on hash hits—O(n log n) time with O(n) hash-map space when hashing is good.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions binary search on length plus rolling-hash duplicate check, and O(n log n) / O(n) complexity.

probes: How do you find the shortest string to prepend to make a palindrome using KMP’s LPS?

hints.1: You need the longest prefix of s that is already a palindrome.
hints.2: Form one string from s, a separator, and reverse(s), then read the last LPS entry.
hints.3: combined = s + "#" + reverse(s); longest palindromic prefix length = lps.back(); reverse s[that_length...] and prepend it to s.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: For a single pattern, KMP or Z both give deterministic O(n+m) via pattern preprocessing and Rabin–Karp is rarely faster; use rolling hash when you need many queries, duplicate-substring search, or multidimensional matching across starting positions.

Manacher finds the longest palindromic substring in optimal O(n) by reusing mirror radii inside the rightmost palindrome boundary; expand-around-centre is O(n²) but is almost always an acceptable interview fallback if Manacher’s details are forgotten.

A large prime modulus reduces collisions, but on adversarial tests (e.g. LeetCode) double hashing with two different moduli makes a collision in both practically impossible; always verify character-by-character on hash equality because of spurious collisions.

gotchas.trap: Treating equal Rabin–Karp hashes as a confirmed match without comparing characters.
gotchas.correction: Hashes can collide (spurious collisions); always verify the window character by character, and use a large prime M—or double hashing—to minimise collisions.

gotchas.trap: Assuming Rabin–Karp is always linear like KMP.
gotchas.correction: Average case is O(n + m), but many spurious collisions (e.g. searching "AAA" in "AAAAA") degrade to O(n · m) worst case.

gotchas.trap: Forgetting to fix a negative rolling-hash value after modulo arithmetic when sliding the window.
gotchas.correction: After the remove/shift/add update, if the hash is negative, add MOD to convert it back to a positive residue.

gotchas.trap: Building s + reverse(s) for shortest palindrome / LPS without a separator.
gotchas.correction: Use combined = s + "#" + reverse(s); the "#" prevents the matched prefix from overlapping the suffix beyond the original string’s length.

gotchas.trap: In Z-algorithm, copying Z[i - l] unchanged whenever i ≤ r.
gotchas.correction: Only initialize Z[i] = min(Z[i - l], r - i + 1), then extend naively past r if possible—matches are not guaranteed beyond the current window.
